verdict.reasoning: Patient reports “over the past few days, I've noticed my skin is sore and red” and “It's very itchy,” indicating widespread itchy, sore, red skin for a few days.
Location: “It's all over my chest, my hands and arms, especially inside of the elbows.” The inside of the elbows corresponds to the antecubital fossae and is noted as the worst area.
Patient/doctor interchange: “It's very itchy and dry. ... All over my body, itchy and dry.”
When asked if lesions are weeping: “Is it weeping?...” Patient: “No.”
When asked about thickened/darkened skin (lichenification): “Is there any thickened skin…?” Patient: “No. No, I don't think so.”
History: “Have you had something like this in the past? … I have Eczema in the past.” and “Do you think this is similar to your usual eczema or is it worse? … I think it's gotten worse.”
Systemic symptoms: “Otherwise, other than those rash, you're feeling well in yourself, there's no temperature…?” Patient does not object, implying no fever.
Same sentence: “there's no temperature, no joint pains?” followed by agreement; this supports denial of arthralgia.
Patient: “Yes, I have Eczema in the past.”
Patient: “I have asthma…”
Patient: “Usually I use a cream called Dipro Base.”
Patient: “In the shower. I use something called Dermal.”

Discussion: “Have you ever used steroids…? … Yes, you used it… Which one… Hydrocortisone, does that ring a bell? Yeah. So you're using the hydrocortisone?” indicating over‑the‑counter hydrocortisone cream use.
Asthma meds: “So what medications are you using for asthma? … the blue inhaler… So you just use it on and off? … Yeah, yeah, yeah.” The blue inhaler implies salbutamol used as needed.
Antihistamines: “I realized I've tried also antihistamines and didn't work.” and “which one did you try? … like cetrazene? Yeah, yeah, yeah.”
Allergies: “Do you have any allergies to any medication at all? … No, no allergies.”
Family history: “in my family there is hypothyroidism and migraine. My mother has migraine.” and clarified: “Who has hypothyroidism? … My mother.”
Same segment: “My mother has migraine.”
The transcript contains no discussion of occupation, living situation, smoking, alcohol, or other social history, so stating that social history was not discussed is accurate.

Doctor summarizes “extensive eczema” with widespread involvement and pruritus (“It's very itchy”), no weeping and no thickened/darkened skin, and no systemic signs, consistent with a widespread, pruritic, non‑infected atopic dermatitis flare.
Asthma: uses blue inhaler “on and off” and confirms breathing is okay except “only when I have a flare,” which is consistent with stable asthma managed with as‑needed SABA.
Plan: “You still need to continue on your emollients like the dermal soap and as well as the depravate [Diprobase].”

Plan: “You might probably need a bit more stronger one like betno weight or something like that… we will try with some Bettner weight first… You have to use it twice a day for the next couple of weeks.” This matches betnovate twice daily for ~2 weeks.
Plan: “you would probably need some antihistamines which I'm going to prescribe… it's called the antihistamine it's called fexofenadine.”
The transcript does not mention stopping or replacing the over‑the‑counter hydrocortisone during betnovate use; only addition of betnovate is discussed.
Advice: “If there's no improvement, you need to get back to us. Or if you have any kind of adverse reaction, like an allergic reaction… you need to get in touch with us.”

The doctor says, “If things are getting worse in the next two weeks, call us beforehand. Otherwise, wait for two weeks, take the medication and the cream,” but does not schedule or explicitly plan a routine review appointment in 2 weeks.
There is no explicit instruction in the plan to continue salbutamol; asthma medications are only described in the history section.
Plan: “we are going to send off the prescription to your pharmacy. It looks like Boots on the systems, is that correct? … So I'll send it across to Boots and it will be there for collecting.”
Follow‑up: “If there's no improvement, you need to get back to us. Or if you have any kind of adverse reaction… you need to get in touch with us.”
A specific scheduled review in 2 weeks is not arranged; only advice to wait two weeks while using treatment and to contact sooner if worsening is given.
